Both heads snapped toward the sound. Jake winced. Meg didn’t move. The scream faded. Static flickered faintly in the ceiling lights. Meg stared at the far wall, her knuckles white where they gripped the side of the generator casing. “You said he’s cuffed to something?” she asked, voice quieter now. Jake nodded, his tone easing. “Yeah. Furniture in the room is metal. It’s catching the static. Every time Herman uses one of those wide-area blasts? It jumps to the closest ground.” Meg looked down, her expression unreadable. “And the closest ground is him.” “Exactly.” She was silent for a beat. Then: “I sent Claudette that way a while ago..” Jake’s stomach dropped. “She’s probably already started on one of the gens in the cluster,” Meg continued, voice tighter now. “If he gets close again—” “Leon’s gonna take the hit.” Meg’s jaw clenched. “Alright,” she said, turning back to the generator with a new focus. “I’ll keep Claudette off that side. No sense having her wander into the blast zone blind.” She shot Jake a sharp look. “Whatever the hell you’re doing? Do it fast.” Jake resumed his search with renewed urgency, ducking into room after room along the looping hallways. Most of the spaces were empty beyond any kind of function — overturned chairs, snapped monitors, half-empty toolboxes filled with bent screwdrivers and loose screws. Nothing useful. He was making faster time than expected, but the lack of options gnawed at him. Either the keys were stashed somewhere absurd, or they were being moved. Neither possibility sat well. He passed a hallway junction, angling toward the rotunda. A curved staircase led him up to the observation deck, open windowpanes staring down into the morbid circle of chairs below. Inside, the air felt stale, dead with disuse. The counters were littered with cracked keyboards, old monitors flickering with distorted light, and piles of paperwork that had long since succumbed to mold and rust. He yanked open one drawer and was met with a heap of rusted scissors and half-melted gauze pads. Another offered nothing but paperwork warped from water damage. A third, hidden behind a binder the size of his head, held an anatomy chart rolled tight — half its labels missing or burned away. “Jesus, what is this place even for? ” he muttered, slamming the drawer shut. “What is all this shit? Does the Fog just litter junk around for aesthetic ?” He reached for the next set, only for a spark to pop at his wrist — a thin arc of static snapping between the drawer handle and the nearest keyboard, shorting out with a loud pop and the smell of singed plastic. Jake hissed and jerked back. The air was humming again. Jake’s chest tightened. The next scream came seconds later. Short. Sharp. Choked off halfway like it had been startled out of someone mid-breath. Jake froze, eyes scanning the walls, listening. He couldn’t tell how far away it was — but that tone ... That one hadn’t been random. That was targeted. Jake’s breath caught. His head whipped toward the windows, hoping for a glimpse of movement — but the angle was garbage. The rotunda’s observation deck didn’t give a clean sightline into the corridors, and the overhead lights only deepened the shadows. Frustrated, he spun back toward the desk, eyes catching on the half-lit monitors still glitching faintly in the corner. The system was a mess — screens frozen mid-frame, others jittering like broken film reels — but they were still active. Jake stabbed at the keyboard, flipping through camera feeds. Blank hallway. Broken med bay. Rusted bathroom. Most were distorted messes — glitched overlays and flickering grayscale. But one held, the feed jittering every few seconds like a scratched DVD. Leon. He was still in the same position Jake had left him in — kneeling against the cabinet, arm stretched upward at a brutal angle. But now his body had slumped. The cuff kept him tethered upright, but his spine had curled in on itself, his free hand clenched in a death grip against the front of his vest. Whether he was shaking from pain or it was just the jitter of the monitor, Jake couldn’t tell. But the stillness in him was wrong. The kind of still you only got when moving made things worse. Jake leaned in closer, one hand bracing the side of the monitor. Another feed flickered to life beside it. A hallway view. Empty — except for one figure dead center, face tilted up toward the lens. Herman. He stood perfectly still, framed in grainy grayscale, the fringe of his coat swaying slightly as though moved by an unseen wind. His mouth curled upward, and even through the distortion, the expression was unmistakable. He knew. He was watching the camera. Watching Jake. Jake’s stomach turned to ice. The Doctor raised one hand, flexing as he built up a charge alone the arm, then placed his palm flat against the wall beside him. The screen scrambled briefly from the static burst, but Jake didn’t need the audio feed. The scream that followed echoed through the halls. Jake gripped the counter so hard his knuckles went white. He knew. He knew what he was doing. Leon wasn’t just collateral damage anymore — he was bait. And Herman was hitting him just hard enough to make sure someone else came running. Three more rooms. Three more dead ends. Jake found himself in what looked like a side office near the rear of the wing — smaller than the others, but strangely pristine. The floors were clean. The desk was polished.
